cells.tense: You are here at the completion, and you are letting it finish.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: Name what you gave in something that has finished, and name what came back. Add the two up out loud if that helps. Once the scales read even, set them down and leave them.
cells.core:
You can watch something end without rushing it or holding it back. What's finished gets to be finished, and what's next doesn't have to be named yet. You know when a thing has run its course, and you act on that instead of waiting for someone to hand you a reason.

Exchange is what keeps an ending clean for you. You give what the closing asks and take what's yours from it without holding a running tally past the point where the two sides match. This week, take stock of one finished thing — what went out, what came in — and when the count levels, put it down. You'll notice the pattern underneath sooner once the balancing isn't running in the background.
cells.sheetLine: The ending stays clean while give and take stay level.
cells.verb: ending what is finished so the next thing can begin
cells.place: where you see the shape of things without their contents

cells.tense: You are bracing for a change you can't write yet, so you end things first.
cells.act: feel it alongside them and keep your own side
cells.ask: Before you cut the next thing loose, sit with someone it touches and feel what they're carrying without losing your own footing. Stay there a while. Decide nothing yet.
cells.core:
You're clearing things before they've had their season. A friendship, a role, a plan — when it gets tense, you end it, and the ending feels like freedom. It isn't quite. It's the relief of not having to wait for something you can't control, and the relief is what you're chasing, not the ending itself.

The pattern you're good at seeing has gone thin: you're reading the shape of what's coming more than what's actually here. Sit with somebody this touches and feel their side without dissolving into it. You don't have to keep the thing. You just have to stop ending it alone.
cells.sheetLine: You end things early so the future can't end them for you.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Something wants you and you've been slow to answer. Take a step toward it today — send the message, make the call, look it up. One step only, then stop.
cells.core:
Something in your life has already ended, and you're still tending it. You give it names — loyalty, patience, not being the kind of person who walks away — and the names hold it upright. From the outside it looks like standing very still in a room that's already been emptied.

A pull in you points somewhere else. You can feel the direction without having said it. Follow that one step today. Not because the old thing was wrong, and not to prove anything. Because the part of you that knows what it wants is the part that knows when something's over, and it hasn't been consulted.
cells.sheetLine: You're loyal to something that's already gone.

cells.tense: You are writing the next chapter without noticing that the last one ended.
cells.act: set one rule that makes the rest easier
cells.ask: Take a foggy stretch of your life and set down a single rule for it — what comes first, what's over, what you stop doing. One line, one page, kept where you'll see it.
cells.core:
You rearrange your life constantly and call it normal. People leave, jobs shift, plans change, and you've already moved the furniture before anyone asked whether you noticed. The pattern-sense is strong: you see how things fit together. What you don't see is that a few of the pieces you keep fitting were for a shape you've outgrown.

Give that stretch one rule it can live by — a line about what comes first or what you've stopped doing. It won't fix the fog, and it isn't meant to. It puts the ending somewhere other than a feeling you keep stepping around. The shape you draw is the one you go by.
